transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-08-24 15:30 PDT | Duration: 47m | Recording: yes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Sam Torres (Meridian Head of Search), Leila Gomez (Eng Manager), Ravi Desai (Infra Lead)

Summary:
Sam and team are exploring options to replace a brittle in-house hybrid search stack. Primary goals: scale embedding fanout across geo replicas, reduce tail latency for re-rank, and decide where to run inference (hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC) given PCI-like compliance and EU residency for some catalogs. Cost sensitivity for peak holiday traffic is high.

Topics: embedding dimensionality, sharding and shard routing, hybrid top-k vs single-pass rerank, routing/fallback policies, private deployment constraints (VPC/KMS), and benchmarking plan.

[00:00] Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll do a 1 min agenda—intros from us, quick background on your current stack, then dig into throughput and hosting constraints, and wrap with next steps. Priya from my side will cover perf patterns.
[00:23] Sam Torres: Hey, thanks. Quick context: Meridian runs an internal retrieval stack—Elastic for inverted, custom vector store for embeddings. We do a fanout of 12 shards for larger catalogs, embeddings are 1536d right now from a LLM-provided embedder. Rerank is a separate step using a 7B model on GPUs, but it's getting expensive and tail latency spikes during promo windows.
[00:55] Priya Nair: Got it. When you say tail spikes, what numbers are we talking p95/p99?
[01:02] Sam Torres: p95 around 180ms for vector fetch + 60ms for rerank on avg, p99 goes up to 1.2s on peak days. The rerank step is biggest problem.
[01:12] Leila Gomez: Also want to note we have EU data residency constraints for product catalogs sold in EU — can't have embeddings stored in US-only managed DBs without contractual controls.
[01:23] Alex Chen: Understood. We often see two patterns: 1) hybrid top-k then rerank (reduce rerank calls), or 2) single-pass heavy model with bigger fanout and more compute. Both have tradeoffs. Priya, want to take the perf tradeoff?
[01:35] Priya Nair: Sure. Broadly, embedding dims matter: 1536 dims is common but if you can move to 768 or 384 you save memory and network bandwidth; quality drop depends on your rerank stage. For rerank, batching, KV cache for autoregressive models and quantization can cut cost but affects latency.
[02:10] Ravi Desai: We are leaning to keep rerank but want to move host location — either Redwood Hosted in eu-west or Redwood Dedicated in our VPC; private on-prem is a last resort. We need KMS integration and audit logs.
[02:25] Alex Chen: Redwood Dedicated gives you reserved capacity with VPC peering and KMS/HSM integration — audit logs and compliance add-ons are standard. Hosted eu-west can be quicker to start but we'd need to set data residency guardrails.
[02:40] Sam Torres: Pricing question: how does dedicated reserved capacity compare to hosted for bursty traffic? We have 10x swing in Q4.
[02:50] Priya Nair: Dedicated is great for predictable throughput; you can configure burst policies. For bursty, a hybrid routing policy (hosted fallback) is common: keep canary reserved capacity for base load and overflow to hosted. That keeps unit-cost lower for baseline but avoids saturation.
[03:20] Leila Gomez: Do you support hybrid routing for the same model version? Like pins to a quantized variant when on hosted?
[03:26] Priya Nair: Yes — we can route by policy: prefer dedicated -> if queue depth or latency crosses SLO then route to hosted quantized variant. We maintain model versioning so signal stays consistent. There can be subtle quality diffs you'll want to measure.
[03:45] Sam Torres: About vector DB integration — we use a custom store; we could move to an off-the-shelf DB, but prefer to keep our index. How would Redwood fit?
[03:56] Alex Chen: Redwood treats the model layer as separate; you can keep your vector DB. Common integrations: we call your vector DB for top-k IDs then call Redwood for embeddings or rerank. We also support retrieving embeddings from Redwood if you want managed storage, but since you have residency concerns, likely keep your DB.
[04:20] Priya Nair: A low-latency pattern is to do nearest-neighbor search in your vector DB (top-200), then a lightweight embed similarity pass in Redwood to prune to top-20 and then run a rerank decider only on top-20. That cuts rerank cost sharply.
[04:45] Ravi Desai: Network egress and tokenization cost — what are typical numbers for a top-200 -> rerank 20 flow?
[04:53] Priya Nair: It depends on model and prompt size. Roughly, top-200 fetch cost is DB IO; rerank token counts usually small if you send only short context; you'd pay per-token on hosted. On dedicated, it's mostly infrastructure cost amortized. We'll run exact numbers on your sample dataset.
[05:15] Sam Torres: One concern: embedding dimensionality and consistency across vendors. If we switch embedder to a 384-d to save cost, will retrieval quality tank for cold queries?
[05:26] Priya Nair: Usually you evaluate on held-out search tasks. Some customers compress with product-specific fine-tuning and get away with 384 for many queries. We recommend running A/B on real traffic for relevancy delta. Redwood Optimize can suggest dimension/quantization tradeoffs for your workload.
[05:50] Leila Gomez: Security: If we go Dedicated in our VPC, how are keys managed? We need KMS + HSM option and ability to rotate keys.
[05:59] Alex Chen: Dedicated and Private support KMS integrations; HSM options for enterprise tiers. Key rotation and audit logs are supported — we'll share the SOC2 section and the private deployment checklist after this call.
[06:12] Sam Torres: About latency: we observed rerank p99 spikes due to KV cache misses — do you have suggestions for cache warmers or code patterns?
[06:20] Priya Nair: KV cache (for decoder-only models) depends on seq length. You can prefetch common prefixes or use small model warmers. Also Redwood's runtime supports continuous batching and early-exit rerank heuristics. For high-QPS you can dedicate a warmed pool.
[06:40] Ravi Desai: If we keep our vector DB shards, any recommendations on sharding/replica placement to reduce cross-region fanout? We have EU and US catalogs.
[06:49] Priya Nair: Geo-aware routing: route user queries to region-local vector DB + local dedicated inference when possible. For cross-region queries you can replicate lightweight indexes or async mirror. We usually advise partitioning by catalog to avoid wide fanouts.
[07:10] Sam Torres: What's the operational overhead of managing model variants and rollouts? We want predictable behavior during promos.
[07:18] Alex Chen: Redwood Console has rollouts (canary, A/B) and automatic fallback policies. You can pin traffic percentages and set automatic rollback on quality regressions. We'll show demo on deep-dive.
[07:33] Leila Gomez: Do you have benchmarks for 1536d vs 768d embeddings on recall for e-commerce taxonomy?
[07:40] Priya Nair: Not for your exact taxonomy; we can run evaluations on your labeled set. Public benchmarks exist but your SKU semantics matter; we'll run a quick eval as part of the pilot.
[07:55] Sam Torres: Can you outline the pilot you recommend? We want quick signals before Q4 planning.
[08:02] Alex Chen: Pilot: 1) Send sample dataset and query logs (anonymized). 2) Redwood runs a 100k query throughput test on Dedicated with your model and a hosted fallback scenario. 3) Evaluate recall/precision lift from rerank at different cutoffs (top-50 -> 10), 4) cost/latency projection for Q4. Estimated 2-3 weeks.
[08:28] Leila Gomez: That timeline sounds fine. For the throughput test, do you need us to dockerize anything?
[08:34] Priya Nair: No, we'll run on Redwood with your embedding model container or using a recommended open model. If you want to test your proprietary embedder, you can provide a container image or we can accept embeddings (vector files) and run rerank tests.
[08:50] Ravi Desai: Networking: how does VPC peering work for Dedicated? We need to avoid opening public endpoints.
[08:58] Alex Chen: Dedicated supports VPC peering and private link; no public endpoints required. For Hosted fallback we can use outbound-only proxied calls or a small egress NAT with agreed controls. We'll include the network diagram in the checklist.
[09:18] Sam Torres: About costs: will Redwood provide modeling for reserved capacity vs on-demand?
[09:24] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll provide a cost projection sheet showing per-token and per-hour reserved cost and break-even points for varying QPS. We'll include burst strategies.
[09:35] Leila Gomez: Any gotchas with quantized models and re-rank quality? We worry quantization might alter top-k order.
[09:42] Priya Nair: Quantization often gives great throughput gains; you should evaluate quality on your queries. We can run a small eval comparing FP16 vs 4-bit quantized variants. For mission-critical ranking it's common to keep a high-precision variant for canary and only route less critical traffic to quantized variants.
[10:05] Sam Torres: Competitors question — we've looked at Pinecone for storage + a separate rerank infra — what advantage would Redwood give?
[10:14] Alex Chen: Redwood unifies the serving/runtime and routing; rather than stitching separate vendors, you get integrated fallback, cost-aware routing, and a console with cost/latency breakdown per token and per-route. That visibility helps optimize holiday traffic.
[10:36] Priya Nair: Also we provide suggestions via Redwood Optimize for batching/quantization and can run quality regressions tied to prompt sets.
[10:45] Sam Torres: Cool. Any immediate risks you see for our setup?
[10:49] Priya Nair: The big risk is not testing with real traffic distribution — synthetic tests can miss tail patterns. Also ensure you have observability on top-k drift after embedding changes. We'll instrument that in the pilot.
[11:05] Alex Chen: Recap of next steps — Redwood send security & deployment checklist and cost template by 2026-08-27, Meridian share sample data by 2026-08-28, Priya run sample throughput by 2026-09-02, schedule deep-dive week of 2026-09-07.
[11:20] Sam Torres: Sounds good. One small ask: can you include examples of routing policy configs? We have a platform team that likes concrete policy YAMLs.
[11:27] Alex Chen: Yes, we'll include sample routing configs and a short runbook.
[11:33] Leila Gomez: Thanks everyone, this was helpful.
[11:37] Alex Chen: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invites.

End of transcript.
